lines.note: Como papel continues the paste-application example from f191. Cha and komugi introduce grinding tea and wheat, another hiku sense.
The divided nadeuo is preserved even though nado would be expected; the scan has de here. Moer explains grinding tea and wheat, and cha is embedded Japanese.
Shibu and sumi are applied with a brush. The Portuguese pincellada is physically divided, with a visible terminal division sign.

runs.text: da com çumo de figos de Iapão, tinta, &c.

lines.note: The brush coating uses Japanese-fruit juice or ink. This explains the preceding objects without replacing the dictionary's fruit description with a modern botanical term.
Kusa o hiku is pulling weeds out by hand. This is the literal pulling sense with vegetation as object.
Ke o hiku is drawing ruled lines, as lançar riscas explains. Sa- starts sakana in the next example.

runs.text: Repartir pellos que estão à me-

lines.note: Sakana o hiku is distributing food to those at table, rather than the unrelated modern reading 'pull a fish'.

runs.text: ſa com as faxis algũa couſa de comer. ¶

lines.note: Food is distributed using hashi, here faxis in a Portuguese plural construction. Yu begins the subsequent bathing example.

runs.text: Lauar o corpo com agoa quente.

lines.note: Yu o hiku is glossed as washing the body with hot water; this completes the broad first hiku entry.
This independent hiku entry concerns subtracting in accounts. Preserve the printed comparison with multiplication, even if it seems imprecise mathematically.

runs.text: de multiplicar. ¶ Item, Deſcontar nas di-

lines.note: A further application is deducting debts; di- begins dividas below. Item introduces this additional sense.
Sashihiki is explicitly preferred by Meliùs for the accounting sense. It is a cross-reference, not Portuguese text.
Another hiku means sawing. Quo is the printed object form; the following wood/tree gloss guides interpretation without silently changing it to another romanization.

runs.text: Serrar pao, ou aruore. ¶ Item, Fazer

lines.note: Sawing wood or a tree is followed by an additional sense of working material on a lathe.
Juzu o hiku describes turning beads. I is consonantal in this word, and contas refers to beads rather than accounting here.
Ao torno finishes the bead-turning example; its short independent crop is not a heading or catchword.
Hikyaku is a courier, corresponding to the compact Portuguese correo gloss.
Hikiagaru here describes soldiers withdrawing to higher ground, rather than merely any upward pull.
The destination is a high place; this line completes both soldados and the retirement definition.
Hikiageru is pulling upward, with uru/eta showing the older inflectional paradigm.
Hikiau is reciprocal pulling, each person drawing toward their own side. The inflectional long vowels are preserved from the marked types.

runs.text: ra ſua banda. ¶ Item, Peſar igualmente

lines.note: Each pulls toward their side; the additional sense concerns equal weight, continuing onto the following line.
Loads on both sides balance. Hikiawanu ni introduces a load that does not balance, with negative -nu.
Ja supplies the copula in hikiawanu ni ja. The Portuguese confirms a load unequal in weight.
Hikiakeru means pulling open. The following example elaborates opening sliding paper doors.

runs.text: Coco caxicono xǒjiuo fiqiaqe fiqiaqe mi

lines.note: Koko kashiko no shōji o hikiake hikiake mi- describes opening paper doors here and there and looking; mi, not ma, belongs to mitarureba below.
Mitarureba completes the act of looking. The Portuguese begins opening doors of paper, with papel divided at the row boundary.

runs.text: pel de hũa, & de outra parte, & vẽdo, & c.

lines.note: Opening doors on both sides and looking explains the Japanese repeated verb. Vẽdo visibly abbreviates vendo.
Hikiatsumeru is gathering by pulling things together; ajuntar is one Portuguese infinitive, not an article plus verb.
Hikiateru is drawing something against another surface. The cited example concerns a sword blade.
Katana o nukidaite, bin ni... describes drawing the sword and bringing it to the temple hair. Binni fits that gloss; burni is OCR noise.
The honorific hikiateraretareba completes the quoted action; Feiq. cites Heike, followed by the book number in editorial type.

runs.text: Deſembainhando a Catana chegou a, & pal-

lines.note: Having drawn the sword, he brought it up and passed it along something. Chegou a forms a verb and pronoun sequence, not the garbled chegeua.

runs.text: ſou a pellos cabellos das fontes pera que melhor

lines.note: The blade is passed over the temple hair so that it cuts better. The line begins the rest of paſſou, continuing the previous row.
Cortasse completes the stated purpose of that action: better cutting. This is the dictionary's explanation, not advice to reproduce it.
Hikiawase here names the opening or joining of armour, a material noun distinct from the following paper and intercession senses.
The second hikiawase is a kind of paper. Its damaged i was read as t by OCR, but the parallel headword and scan support i.
A third hikiawase means intercession or mediation, returning to bringing parties together.
Hikiawasuru as a verb joins two things by drawing them together. Duas is required by the visible Portuguese phrase, not auas.
Sōhō o hikiawasete rihi... brings both parties together to determine right and wrong. Rifi is rihi, not an unconvertible rih fragment.
Rihi o kessuru completes deciding right and wrong; the Portuguese begins the same action of assembling both sides.

runs.text: julgar, ou determinar a justiça, & injustiça.

lines.note: Judging justice and injustice translates rihi o kessuru. The OCR l substitutions are not plausible Portuguese words.
Another sense is comparison or collation. Mi- begins migi, referring to what has been stated above.
Migi no kotowari o hikiawasete kwai zuruni compares the foregoing reasons in understanding them. Final ni is the connective, not mi or a division sign.

runs.text: Ponderando, & cotejando as razoẽs a cima

lines.note: Pondering and comparing the aforementioned reasons is the translation; preserve the printed nasal-vowel placement in razoẽs.
Ni o hiki-awasuru concerns arranging loads. The missing i in the OCR verb is visible and required by the repeated compound.

runs.text: concertar o fato de maneira que peſe igualmẽ

lines.note: The load is arranged so that it weighs equally; igualmẽ continues with te at the top of column 2.
Equal weight on both sides concludes the previous column. Hito o hito ni introduces bringing one person before another, not hito no.
Hiki-awasuru here is introducing people, making one known to another; the phrase crosses the physical line break.

runs.text: outro, ou leualo diante dalguem pera o conhe-

lines.note: Another person is made known or brought into someone's presence. Outro and dalguem repair OCR omissions within an otherwise clear sentence.
Conhecerem completes the purpose of the introduction: that they may become acquainted.
Hikiaonokeru is turning something face upward. Its old aono- form need not be modernized to aomuke-.

runs.text: pera riba, ou a alguem cõ o roſto pera cima.

lines.note: The object may be a person with their face upward. This specifies the orientation intended by virar.
Hikikaburu means drawing a covering over oneself. The headword's missing i is faint, but supported by the visible spacing and neighbouring compound forms.
One pulls the covering toward oneself; puxandoa and perasi retain the printed fusion of the Portuguese pronouns.

runs.text: Fiqicacari, u, l, Ficcacari, u, atta.

lines.note: Hikikakaru/hikkakaru is getting caught. Atta is the expected past ending and is also supported by the repeated t strokes.
A dōbuku garment supplies the example of something getting entangled; the long-o mark belongs to the Japanese noun.
Dōbuku nado ibara ni hiki kakatta says the garment caught on thorns. Prendeoſe is the Portuguese predicate and Dǒ begins its embedded garment name.
The garment name finishes before thickets or thorns explain ibara. Keep that cross-line Japanese fragment in roman type.
Hikikakusu is hiding something by pulling it out of view. Preserve the source's uita inflection rather than regularizing it.
Hikikagameru is bending or folding, repaired from an OCR c/e confusion. The following example tests the reading against bent legs.
Ashi o hiki kagamuru means bending one's legs or feet; dobrar repeats the general bending gloss.
Entortar os pés is the alternative explanation. The printed o in entortar corrects the OCR a.

runs.text: Doença que procede do àr, ou vento.

lines.note: Hikikaze is a sickness attributed to air or wind. Àr is an accented Portuguese word, not dr.
Hikikakeru begins with drawing earth as with a hoe. The implement enxada is divided over the physical lines.

runs.text: xada pella terra botar emcima dalgũa couſa,

lines.note: Earth is thrown onto something by drawing the hoe through it. Emcima retains the joined printed spelling.

runs.text: ou ao pè da aruore, &c. ¶ Item puxando

lines.note: The earth can be placed at a tree's foot; pè has a grave, not a nasal tilde. Item begins another covering application.

runs.text: como por roupa, ou outra couſa por ſobreſi,

lines.note: Pulling clothing or another thing over oneself gives another sense of the compound, connected by the infinitive construction above.

runs.text: ou puxando por alguem porlhe a cabeça, &c.

lines.note: The example can also involve pulling a person toward oneself and putting their head somewhere. Cabeça is the visible noun.
The head rests on the knees. Sakamogi begins the next example, referring to a defensive timber barrier.
Sakamogi o hikikakuru is explained by setting timber or trees in place; Porpaos remains the very tight printed sequence.

runs.text: mos, & eſgalhos ao derredor da fortaleza,

lines.note: Branches and projecting limbs surround the fortress, clarifying how the barrier functions.

runs.text: ou noutra parte pera não paſſarem os imigos.

lines.note: The barrier prevents enemies from passing. Imigos is retained as the historical spelling, not modernized to inimigos.
Mi ni hikikakete chisō serareta describes generous treatment as of oneself. Chiſô, not chilô, supplies the recognizable hospitality noun.

runs.text: me gaſalhado como a ſua propria peſſoa.

lines.note: The host treated me as his own person. Gasalhado expresses that welcome, completing fez-me across the line break.
Hikikatamukeru is inclining something by drawing it; the gloss includes a following feminine couſa, and its algũa is fully visible.

runs.text: couſa puxando por ella, ou perſuadindo in-

lines.note: Physical pulling is extended to persuasion. Inclinar divides at the end of the row without creating a new lexical entry.
Inclining someone by persuasion finishes the figurative sense of the preceding verb.
Hikikaeru is changing or exchanging; Per met. introduces the figurative application rather than a Japanese expression.
Shindai o hiki kayuru means changing one's life or circumstances. The whole Japanese example is roman; Mudar a vida is its Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Mudar o traio como fazẽ as figu

lines.note: Another application is changing costume, as theatrical characters do. Figu- continues into figuras below.

runs.text: ras no auto. Itẽ. Empreſtar. i,

lines.note: Characters in a play finish the costume example. Lending is then equated with tori kayuru, another Japanese expression.
Hikikaete is the adverbial 'on the contrary', a lexicalized connective distinct from the verb's literal exchange sense.
Hikikaesu is turning or pulling something back. Eita is preserved in the supplied inflectional notation.
Turning something backward completes tornar...pera tras. It is the continuation of the preceding entry.
Hikikazuku means pulling a cover over oneself, with zzu rendered as historical dzu in the kana aid.
Hikicha is ground tea; the Portuguese moido defines the result of grinding rather than tea as a general drink.
Hikichigaeru here concerns crossing the front panels of a garment. The specific orientation is developed below.

runs.text: teira do veſtido ſobre a outra eſquerda as a-

lines.note: One front lies over the other, left side, in reverse order. Do vestido, not ao, identifies the garment's front portion.

runs.text: ueſſas do que cuſtumão os Iapões. Vt,

lines.note: The arrangement is opposite Japanese custom, according to this gloss. Qi- begins kirumono in the example.
Kirumono o hiki chigayuru supplies the clothing example. The final uru is supported by the verb paradigm and visible types.
Hikichigiru means tearing off by pulling. The compound's g is linguistically important and is retained.

runs.text: ou cortar como corda, ou couſa que està co-

lines.note: A cord or something sewn together exemplifies what can be torn apart; co- belongs to cosida below.
Cosida e pegada finishes the sewn/attached description. The separate lower Fiqi is the catchword, not another body row.
